'''''Tamarix chinensis''''' is a species of [[flowering plant]] in the family ''[[Tamaricaceae]]''.<ref name=POWO>{{cite web |url= https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:828082-1 |title= Tamarix chinensis Lour. |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=n.d. |website=Plants of the World Online |publisher=The Trustees of the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew |access-date=July 18, 2025}}</ref><ref name=COL>{{cite web |url= https://www.catalogueoflife.org/data/taxon/7BJ8N |title= Tamarix chinensis Lour. |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=n.d. |website=Catalogue of Life |publisher=Species 2000 |access-date=July 18, 2025}}</ref> It is sometimes referred to by the common names '''five-stamen tamarisk'''<ref>{{PLANTS|id=TACH2|taxon=Tamarix chinensis|accessdate=8 December 2015}}</ref> and '''Chinese tamarisk'''<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |accessdate=2014-10-17 }}</ref> or '''saltcedar'''. It is native to [[China]] and [[Korea]], and it is known in many other parts of the world as an [[introduced species]] and sometimes an [[invasive species|invasive]] [[noxious weed]]. It easily inhabits moist habitat with [[soil salinity|saline soils]]. It may grow as a [[tree]] with a single trunk or as a [[shrub]] with several spreading erect branches reaching 6 metres or more in maximum height. It has been known to reach 12 metres.<ref name=shep>Sheppard, W. D. (2008). [http://www.fs.fed.us/rm/pubs_other/wo_AgricHandbook727/wo_AgricHandbook727_1087_1088.pdf ''Tamarix chinensis''.] In: Bonner, F. T., et al. ''The Woody Plant Seed Manual''. Agric. Handbook No. 727. Washington, DC. USDA, Forest Service. p. 1087-1088.</ref> It has reddish, brown, or black bark. The small, multibranched twigs are covered in small lance-shaped, scale-like leaves which are no more than about 3 mm long. The [[inflorescence]] is a dense [[raceme]] of flowers a few cm long. Each fragrant flower has five petals which are usually pink but range from white to red.

This tamarisk [[Hybrid (biology)|hybridizes]] commonly with ''T. ramosissima'' in the North American invasion<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Gaskin |first=John F. |last2=Schaal |first2=Barbara A. |date=2002-08-20 |title=Hybrid Tamarix widespread in U.S. invasion and undetected in native Asian range |url=https://www.pnas.org/doi/full/10.1073/pnas.132403299 |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=99 |issue=17 |pages=11256–11259 |doi=10.1073/pnas.132403299 |pmc=123243 |pmid=12177412}}</ref>.

It has become an aggressive invader of wildlands in the southwestern United States, where it was once planted as an [[ornamental plant]].<ref name=shep/> It reproduces [[vegetative reproduction|vegetatively]] from its roots and also from its foliage if it happens to be covered by soil, as in sediment-rich flooding.<ref name=shep/> It also reproduces by its seed, which are tiny and tufted with hairs, easily [[biological dispersal|dispersing]] on the wind.<ref name=shep/> Despite its reputation as a noxious weed, the tree can be useful for wood, in [[honey]] production, and as a nesting site for various birds.<ref name=shep/>

In its native habitat in China the plant forms thickets that act as useful barriers on the margins of waterways, including saline ocean shores.<ref>{{cite journal |author=Cui, B. |year=2010 |title=Responses of saltcedar (''Tamarix chinensis'') to water table depth and soil salinity in the Yellow River Delta, China |journal=Plant Ecology |volume=209 |issue=2 |pages=279–290 |doi=10.1007/s11258-010-9723-z|s2cid=12541544 |display-authors=etal}}</ref>
